610.title: Evening prayer
610.hook: Jacob's prayer, said as night falls
610.howItsDone: Maariv is said after nightfall: Barchu, the Shema with its blessings, and the Amidah said silently without a repetition aloud, followed by Aleinu; many people say it right after Mincha, near sunset.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aneni, Elijah's cry answered at the afternoon offering. Your line was heard in the afternoon. Today, the sun goes down.

A young man is running away from home. He's fooled his father, and his brother wants him dead. He walks until the sun sets on the road to Haran: nowhere to sleep, no inn, no tent. He puts a stone under his head and lies down in the open. That night he'll dream of a ladder with angels on it. But before the dream, there's a small verb in the text that the rabbis noticed. And from that verb, they found the evening prayer.
screen: `RUNNING AWAY FROM HOME.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `BEFORE THE DREAM.`

segments.voice: Genesis, in the old Jewish translation: "And he lighted upon the place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set." Lighted upon, in Hebrew vayifga: he came upon, he met, he ran into. The Talmud, in Berakhot, says that same verb can mean to plead or to pray, and reads it here as prayer. So Abraham has the morning, Isaac the afternoon, and Jacob, alone on the road at sundown, the night. The evening prayer is called Maariv, from its first blessing, which praises God who brings on the evenings, ma'ariv aravim. Some communities call it Arvit, from the same root, evening. Now a surprising piece of history. The Talmud records an argument about whether the evening prayer was required at all. One sage said it was optional; another, an obligation. There's a famous, tense story of the academy's leaders clashing over it. In time, it became a fixed part of every day, but a trace of the argument is still there. At Maariv, the leader doesn't repeat the Amidah aloud, the way they do in the morning and afternoon. Everyone says it silently, and the service moves on. One more detail. The Talmud ties the morning and afternoon prayers to the Temple's two daily offerings. For the night, it can only point to what was left burning on the altar until morning. There was no evening offering of its own. Just, in the story, a person on a road, meeting the place where he stopped.

segments.voice: Wherever you'll be when the light goes, that's your place, the way the roadside was Jacob's; look outside if it's dark, or picture this evening's sunset, and slowly notice the room, the street, the sky. If you pray, offer an evening prayer in any words you have; if not, just meet the place you've landed.
Maariv. The one who brings on evening. The night prayer, traced to Jacob meeting the place at sunset.

611.title: Spread over us
611.hook: lay us down in peace and spread over us your shelter
611.howItsDone: Hashkiveinu is the second blessing after the Shema in the evening service, said every night; on Friday nights its closing changes to 'who spreads the shelter of peace', and many congregations sing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maariv, Jacob's prayer on the road at sundown. Your line was meet the place you've landed. Today, a blessing for the night itself.

For a child, the night's fear is the dark under the bed. Later the list changes. The bill on the counter. The test result that hasn't come. The person who didn't text back. The noise downstairs. In the daytime they're errands; after midnight, with the house quiet, they can get very loud. The evening service has a blessing for exactly that hour. It's said every night, between the Shema and the silent prayer, and it's the one that asks for a roof.
screen: `THE DARK UNDER THE BED.` → `LATER, THE LIST CHANGES.` → `A BLESSING THAT ASKS FOR A ROOF.`

segments.voice: Hashkiveinu means lay us down. The prayer begins, in plain English: lay us down, LORD our God, in peace, and raise us up again, our King, to life. Notice the pair, lying down and getting up. It doesn't ask for a perfect night. It asks to make it through to morning. Then the central image: spread over us your shelter of peace. In Hebrew, sukkat shlomecha. A sukkah, like the booth of the festival. Not a fortress with stone walls; a light hut with leaves for a roof, where you can see the stars through the gaps. Shelter that is real, but fragile. Then the prayer gets specific. It asks to be kept from enemies, from disease, from sword, from hunger and from sorrow, and asks God to remove the adversary from before us and behind us. The night's fears, named one by one. The Talmud calls this blessing a long extension of the blessing about redemption that comes just before it. Some connect it with the first Passover night in Egypt, when families stayed inside their houses while danger passed through the streets. How does it end? On weekdays, in most communities: blessed are you, who guards his people Israel forever. On Friday nights, the ending changes: who spreads the shelter of peace over us, over all his people Israel, and over Jerusalem. On Shabbat, the shelter is the last word.

Under it, name one worry you'll take to bed, say it once plainly, and picture it under the roof with you, covered too.

Your line: spread the shelter. Not a fortress, just a roof of leaves. Day six hundred eleven.

612.title: Counting by night
612.hook: during the Omer, the day's count is said at evening prayer
612.howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until the night before Shavuot, the omer is counted each night after nightfall, usually at the end of Maariv: a blessing, then the day's number in days and weeks. Someone who misses a full day continues counting without the blessing, according to common practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hashkiveinu, lay us down in peace. Your line was spread the shelter. Today, something extra the evening service holds for seven weeks a year.

Days till vacation. Sleeps till a birthday. Weeks till a baby is due. A countdown makes waiting feel like it's going somewhere. For seven weeks every spring, from the second night of Passover until Shavuot, Jewish tradition keeps a different kind of count, out loud, one day at a time. At the end of the evening service, the congregation stops, says a blessing, and announces the number. Today is twelve days, which is one week and five days. And then everyone goes home. Tomorrow night, thirteen.
screen: `COUNTING DOWN TO THINGS.` → `SEVEN WEEKS EVERY SPRING.` → `TODAY IS TWELVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: The count comes from Leviticus. In the old Jewish translation: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the day of rest, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the waving; seven weeks shall there be complete." The sheaf is the omer, a measure of new barley brought to the Temple on the second day of Passover. So the count is called sefirat ha'omer, counting the omer. Forty-nine days, and on the fiftieth, Shavuot, the festival of the wheat harvest and, in Jewish tradition, of receiving the Torah at Sinai. Why count at night? In the Jewish calendar, a day begins at sundown, and the verse says the weeks should be complete, temimot. Count in the morning and you'd miss part of the day. Counting at nightfall catches each day from its very start, so it belongs to Maariv. One rule makes people careful. Forget to count one night, and you can still count the next day, without the blessing. But miss a whole day, and many authorities say you keep counting for the rest of the weeks without saying the blessing. The chain matters. And notice which way it counts. Not down, but up: not days left until Shavuot, but days already lived since Passover. From freedom toward the Torah, step by step. Each number is a small claim: I was here for this one too.

segments.voice: Choose one thing you're in the middle of, days since you started something, weeks you've kept a habit, days on this path, and count it up, not down. Say the number aloud the way the omer is said, today is this many days, and let each one count as a day you showed up.
Sefirat ha'omer. Counting the sheaf: the forty-nine days from Passover to Shavuot, counted up at evening prayer.
Your line: count by night. Up, not down, one day at a time. That's day six hundred twelve.

613.title: Praying alone
613.hook: without ten people some parts are skipped, but the prayer still counts
613.howItsDone: Someone praying without a minyan says the Shema, its blessings and the Amidah in full, and leaves out Barchu, Kedushah, the repetition of the Amidah, the Torah reading and the Kaddish; many try to pray at the same time as their community's service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sefirat ha'omer, the omer counted up at nightfall. Your line was count by night. Today, what happens when you're the only one in the room.

A hospital waiting room at six in the morning. A soldier on a base far from any synagogue. A student in a dorm who just isn't going to make it to services. A grandmother at her kitchen window before anyone else is up. For weeks, this path has walked through the service as a congregation says it: the leader, the answers, the ten. But on any given morning, some Jews pray with a congregation, and some pray by themselves. What happens to the prayer then?
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `A KITCHEN WINDOW.` → `ONE PERSON, ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, what's missing. Jewish law says certain parts are matters of holiness, said only with a minyan of ten. Without ten, you leave out Barchu, the call to prayer. The Kedushah, the holy, holy, holy said standing together. The leader's repetition of the Amidah. The Torah reading. And the Kaddish, met earlier on this path. Those are real losses, and the rabbis didn't pretend otherwise. The Talmud says a prayer said with the community is especially welcome, and encourages someone alone to pray at the same time the congregation does, joined in time if not in place. But here's the other half. The heart of the service, the Shema and the Amidah, is complete when you say it alone. It counts. Fully. And the model for the silent Amidah is one woman praying by herself: Hannah, in the book of Samuel, at the sanctuary in Shiloh, with no one praying alongside her. In the old Jewish translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest who saw her thought she was drunk. The Talmud draws lessons for all prayer from that one scene: pray with intention, move your lips, keep your voice quiet. So the silent Amidah, said by a whole congregation standing together, is built on a woman praying alone. At its quietest moment, the congregation is copying her.
screen: `WITHOUT TEN: NO BARCHU, NO KEDUSHAH.` · `PRAY WHEN THE CONGREGATION PRAYS.` · `THE HEART OF IT IS COMPLETE.` · `HANNAH, ALONE AT SHILOH.` · then, large: `ALONE STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Sit alone with intention, praying if prayer is yours, with no one to follow and no one to answer you. Do what Hannah did: let your lips move, keep your voice too low to hear, and say something real, a thanks, a worry, a hope, and if you like, picture the others in kitchens and waiting rooms doing the same right now.
Praying alone. Without ten, some parts drop away, but the Shema and the Amidah are whole, and the silent prayer is modeled on Hannah.

614.title: Welcoming Shabbat
614.hook: six psalms for six weekdays, begun by the mystics of Safed who went out to greet the day
614.howItsDone: Kabbalat Shabbat is the Friday evening service before Maariv in most communities: Psalms 95–99 and 29, the song Lecha Dodi, then Psalms 92 and 93. Many congregations sing it, and some still begin it outdoors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying alone, and Hannah at Shiloh. Your line was alone still counts. Today, the week ends, and the prayer book changes.

Late Friday afternoon, in a hill town in the Galilee, in the 1500s. A group of scholars and mystics put on white clothes and walk out past the last houses, into the fields, as the sun drops toward the sea. They aren't going anywhere. They're going out to meet someone. The town is Safed, home to a famous circle of Jewish mystics, and the someone they're walking out to greet is the Sabbath itself. Almost every synagogue's Friday night service still carries the shape of that walk.
screen: `FRIDAY, IN SAFED.` → `WHITE CLOTHES, INTO THE FIELDS.` → `GOING OUT TO MEET SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Kabbalat Shabbat means receiving, or welcoming, the Sabbath. The idea is old. The Talmud tells of a sage who wrapped himself in his cloak at sundown on Friday and said: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen. But the service with that name took shape in Safed, in the sixteenth century, among the circle of kabbalists there, and from them it spread around the Jewish world. Its backbone is six psalms, ninety-five through ninety-nine, and twenty-nine: one for each of the six weekdays that have just ended. You walk back through the week, psalm by psalm, before you step into the seventh day. The first is a summons. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 95 begins: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD; let us shout for joy to the Rock of our salvation." The last, Psalm 29, is a thunderstorm: the voice of the LORD, seven times over, upon the waters, breaking the cedars, shaking the wilderness. And then it ends with one word: peace. After the storm of the week, peace. Some say the seven voices match the seven blessings of the Friday night Amidah. Then comes a song, which is tomorrow's lesson, and then the two psalms that belonged to Shabbat long before Safed. Notice the posture. Shabbat isn't a day you fall into when you're tired. It's someone you go out to meet, dressed for it, on time.

segments.voice: Look back at your week one day at a time, the way the six psalms do, and take just one image from each day so far. Then, if you'd like, read Psalm 95 or 29 slowly, or simply say its first line, O come, let us sing, and picture yourself walking out to meet the evening.
Kabbalat Shabbat. Welcoming the Sabbath. Six psalms for six days, from the mystics of Safed who walked out to meet it.

615.title: Come, my beloved
615.hook: Shlomo Alkabetz's song greets Shabbat as a bride; everyone turns to the door at the end
615.tomorrow: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)
615.howItsDone: Lecha Dodi is sung in the Friday evening service after the six psalms of Kabbalat Shabbat; at the last verse the congregation stands, turns to face the entrance, and many bow at 'come, O bride'. Mourners in their first week often enter at this point and are greeted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabbalat Shabbat, six psalms for six days. Your line was welcome the day. Today, the song at the center of that welcome.

At a wedding, every head turns toward the back when the doors open for the bride. On Friday night in a synagogue, the same thing happens with no one at the door. A song has been building, verse after verse. At the last verse, the congregation stands, turns around, and faces the doors at the back. Some bow. Nobody walks in. Nobody needs to. The guest they're turning to greet is the Sabbath, arriving like a bride.
screen: `EVERY HEAD TURNS TO THE DOOR.` → `THE LAST VERSE.` → `NOBODY WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: Lecha dodi means come, my beloved. The refrain goes: come, my beloved, to meet the bride; let us welcome the face of Shabbat. It was written by Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz, one of the kabbalists of Safed from yesterday. He signed it, in a way: the first letters of the first eight verses spell his name, Shlomo Halevi. The words are made almost entirely of older words. Come, my beloved, comes from the Song of Songs. In the old Jewish translation: "Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field." And the bride comes from the Talmud. Yesterday's sage greeted Shabbat as a queen. Another, Rabbi Yannai, put on his Sabbath clothes and said: come, O bride, come, O bride. Then the song turns. Its middle verses aren't about Shabbat at all. They speak to Jerusalem, as if to a city lying in the dust. Shake off the dust, arise. Wake up, wake up, your light has come. A song of hope that the broken will be rebuilt, set inside the welcome of a single day. Then the final verse: come in peace, crown of her husband, ending with that line from the Talmud, come, O bride, come, O bride. That's when everyone turns. Tradition says the kabbalists of Safed sang it out in the fields, facing the setting sun. Indoors, the room faces the door instead. A welcome that once meant walking out now means turning around.

segments.voice: Stand if you can, turn slowly to face the door of the room you're in, and picture something good about to come through it, not a person you're waiting on, but rest, quiet, peace. If you know the words, say come, O bride, softly; if not, just say come in, and bow a little if you like.
Lecha dodi. Come, my beloved. The Safed song that greets Shabbat as a bride, and turns the whole room to the door.

616.title: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)
616.hook: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD", the psalm of the Sabbath day
616.howItsDone: Psalm 92, followed by Psalm 93, closes Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday night and is said again in the Shabbat morning service as the psalm of the day; many congregations sing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lecha Dodi, and the room turning to the door. Your line was shake off the dust, arise. Today, the psalm sung right after the bride arrives.

Here's a small puzzle. There's a psalm the Mishnah calls the Sabbath's song. It says the Levites sang it in the Temple on Shabbat. Jews say it on Friday night and again on Saturday morning. Its title says, in so many words, for the Sabbath day. And then, in the whole psalm, the Sabbath is never mentioned again. No rest, no seventh day, no candles. So what makes it the Sabbath's song?
screen: `THE SABBATH PSALM.` → `SUNG BY THE LEVITES.` → `NEVER MENTIONS THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Psalm 92, in the old Jewish translation, opens with its title: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Then the first line: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD." And it goes on: to declare your lovingkindness in the morning, and your faithfulness in the night. The whole day, held in thanks. Then the psalm notices something hard. The wicked spring up like grass; they seem to be winning. But grass is gone in a season. And the righteous? "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree." Like a cedar in Lebanon: trees that grow slowly and stand a long time. So maybe that's the Sabbath in it. Six days you watch the grass, what's fast, loud, winning this week. On the seventh you look at the trees, what's slow and lasting. The Mishnah offers another answer: a song for the time to come, for a day that will be entirely Sabbath. A world at rest. And a midrash tells a third story. Adam, it says, met his son Cain after the murder of Abel, and learned that Cain had repented and been given another chance. Adam was amazed and said: so great is the power of returning. And he sang this psalm. Some readers hear a second meaning in the opening line. The Hebrew for give thanks, l'hodot, shares its root with the word for confessing, admitting. It is good to give thanks. It is good to own up. After Adam's story, one word can carry both.
screen: `FOR THE SABBATH DAY.` · `MORNING AND NIGHT, IN THANKS.` · `GRASS, AND THE PALM TREE.` · `L'HODOT: THANK, AND CONFESS.` · then, large: `GOOD TO GIVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Look back at the week and find one thing that was slow and good, a tree, not grass: a friendship that held, a habit you kept, a meal someone made. Name it, and say thank you for it, out loud or inside, to God if you pray, or to the person, or simply to the day.
L'hodot. To give thanks: the first word of Psalm 92's opening line, the Sabbath psalm that never mentions the Sabbath.
Your line: good to give thanks. A week of Maariv, Hashkiveinu, the omer, praying alone, Kabbalat Shabbat, Lecha Dodi and Psalm 92. That's six hundred sixteen.
